thread.title: Driving The i-Pace: How Jaguar Hit Tesla Where It Hurts - Tesla, Inc. (NASDAQ:TSLA)

author: Anton Wahlman
title: Driving The i-Pace: How Jaguar Hit Tesla Where It Hurts - Tesla, Inc. (NASDAQ:TSLA)
text:
Since the advent of the Model S in 2012, Tesla (NASDAQ: TSLA ) has been the lone market participant in the premium long-range battery-electric vehicle (BEV) market. The Chevrolet (NYSE: GM ) Bolt arrived on the scene 18 months ago as a non-premium competitor, costing only $37,495 before discounts that are customarily material.
By the end of 2022, there will be at least approximately 150 long-range BEVs in the market, but the first premium competitor to arrive in dealerships is the Jaguar i-Pace? A few days ago, I got to spend a day and a half testing the Jaguar i-Pace to see how it compares to the Tesla Model S and X, as I had driven them before.
I wasn’t alone in getting to drive this car. Over a few weeks, Jaguar had more than 100 journalists, most of whom with considerable experience in evaluating cars against each other, drive the i-Pace in order to render a verdict. I spoke to around 20 of them to varying degrees, and read and watched the reviews that a few of the others produced.
For example, in just the last couple of days, we saw this review from Roman Mica and Nik Miles of TFL Car, the leading car reviewing site on YouTube: here .
We also saw the review from Roberto Baldwin of Engadget : here.
And then there’s one of Elon Musk’s favorite web sites, Ars Technica : here.
Paul Eisenstein is one of the most experienced automotive journalists: here.
Autoblog had an interesting take: here.
I could go on an on. The point is this: Don’t take only my word for it. What I’m about to say was the consensus view of the vast majority of the professional car reviewers - not an outlier opinion.
The other piece of background is Tesla’s warranty exclusions. They basically say that its cars are too fragile to be driven even on a dirt road: here.
All that is made clear by Tesla Model S warranty. Just look at page six: here.
“Driving over uneven, rough, damaged or hazardous surfaces, including but not limited to, curbs, potholes, unfinished roads, debris, or other obstacles, or in competition, racing or autocross or for any other purposes for which the vehicle is not designed.”
So, driving over “uneven, rough” surfaces will kick you out of your Tesla Model S warranty.
Finally, it should be pointed out that the Jaguar i-Pace is not a 100% exact pound-for-pound competitor to any single car in Tesla’s current lineup:
Model S: The Jaguar is shorter and taller, but less expensive.
Model X: The Jaguar is smaller, but less expensive.
Model 3: The Jaguar is taller, available only as all-wheel drive, but more expensive.
The naysayer would therefore say, in the pettiest of manners, that “Jaguar i-Pace doesn’t compete with any Tesla, so it’s irrelevant no matter how good it is.” In my opinion, that makes no sense at all.
Rather, the correct interpretation is that the Jaguar i-Pace competes with all Tesla models to some degree. Yes, the Model 3 has a lower base price - and the S and X have higher base prices. Yes, the Model X buyer might need the extra space. Yes, the Model S buyer might hate the idea of a crossover that’s a little taller.
So yes, there are "some" Tesla buyers who have special needs or constraints that cause them to not consider the Jaguar i-Pace. We have no idea what portion of real or would-be Tesla buyers that is. Is it 50%? More? Less? My sense is that a majority of would-be Tesla buyers would have good reason to consider the Jaguar. The biggest reason "not" to consider the Jaguar would probably be the i-Pace’s $70,495 (before discounts) base price, which is a lot higher than Tesla’s current $50,000 base price for the version of the Model 3 that's actually available for purchase today.
Of course, the Performance version of the Tesla Model 3 starts at $78,000, so that’s about $8,000 more than the Jaguar. I begins production and shipments within weeks from now.
I got to drive the Jaguar i-Pace in a variety of circumstances. Let’s take them in turn.
Wading in up to 50 cm depth:
Building on its Land Rover heritage, and combining it with the sealed battery as well as lacking a sensitive exhaust pipe, the Jaguar i-Pace is certified to go under 50 cm of water. That’s almost 20 inches.
We drove the car on a riverbed, and that might be an unlikely venue for most prospective electric car buyers. However, once every decade or two, you might experience a severe flood, even in a place such as Beverly Hills or New York City. You might just encounter 20 inches of water, even if you’re on asphalt pavement below.
And in that context, ask yourself the question: How much is a flood-damaged Tesla worth? But your Jaguar i-Pace will be fine.
Off-road terrain:
We drove the car on steep off-road mountain sides. The Jaguar’s all-wheel drive system can be set at a constant speed that allows the computer to avoid wheel slip. All you need to do is to steer, and the Jaguar will claw itself up the mountain side. This is clearly well beyond driving on a gravel road, where a Tesla Model S is verboten. It's a new frontier for electric car motoring that some reviewers believe will appeal to many buyers.
And yes, we drove the Jaguar i-Pace on a gravel road too. It was, of course, a piece of cake in comparison.
Racetrack:
The main problem with driving a Tesla on a racetrack is that a Tesla can overheat and go into some form of “limp mode” as a result. That’s why you have to take it easy when driving it on the track, so that the car doesn’t break down: here.
Not so with the Jaguar. I asked Jaguar’s test engineers about the way it manages driving in heat at top speed, and they told me that the car simply does not overheat or go into any “limp mode.” I didn’t get enough number of laps to fully verify that claim, but I drove the car at 208 km/h (as indicated on the speedometer) multiple times and there was no trace of any problem, overheating or otherwise.
On the road:
Of course, most people will drive the car “normally” most of the time. This means a mix of freeways and urban/suburban traffic, including curvy mountainside twisties. As we all know who have driven a Tesla on such regular roads, a Tesla drives very well on these roads. It is certainly as pleasant as just about any other car. Jaguar has no particular advantage over Tesla here.
So therefore, the question here became - given that the Jaguar has so many other tricks up its sleeve when driven off-road, through deep water and on the racetrack - whether the i-Pace can simply match a Tesla when driven on normal roads. The answer is yes, it can. On the whole, the experience of “just driving around” feels very similar to the average of Teslas on the market today.
What about the interior of the Jaguar i-Pace? It’s most similar to the Range Rover Velar, which arrived in the market around August 2017. The controls are a mix of touchscreens, knobs and buttons.
The only thing I didn’t like about the Jaguar’s cockpit was the temperature controls, as I found them not as intuitive as many other “basic” cars. Yes, you will learn them once you figure them out, but they ought to be as intuitive as most basic cars and trucks are.
Jaguar i-Pace also is the first JLR product to come with Android(NASDAQ: GOOG ) (NASDAQ: GOOGL ) Auto and Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ) CarPlay. These features will be delivered via over-the-air (OTA) software update, as the early production cars made in the last couple of months, did not have them. Jaguar did not promise specifically when this OTA arrives, but it seemed imminent - as in this summer.
One really has to wonder how long Tesla can keep up this war against Apple and Google, now that Tesla is the only automaker left to not offer Android Auto or Apple CarPlay. All other automakers ether already have one or both of them in all or some of their cars, or will be pushing it as an update in the coming months.
Jaguar’s integration with Google goes even deeper. Waymo, which is Alphabet’s autonomous car entity, has signed an agreement to make 20,000 Jaguar i-Pace cars that drive themselves, for a Waymo robotaxi fleet. Testing is starting this year, and plan on volume deliveries starting in 2020: here.
Speaking of integration, Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN ) Alexa also is integrated with the Jaguar i-Pace. You can get all sorts of information and bark out orders over this voice assistant. I’m not a fan of any kind of voice assistant - I would rather have them banned in my presence - but at least it is one more example of how much more technologically advanced Jaguar is than Tesla: here.
Then there's the warranty and service. Jaguar includes five years and 60,000 miles worth of free service. Tesla? Not so much. In the Tesla, the four year 50,000 mile plan starts at $2,325, here. Mind you, that’s one year and 10,000 miles less than what’s included in the Jaguar as standard.
One of the impressions that one gets from handling the Jaguar i-Pace is how sturdy some of the details are compared to the various Tesla models. Take the doors for example. The i-Pace has proper door frames around the windows - not those frameless ones. The door handles feel sturdy, are cool to the touch, and work every time - not just sometimes, or get finger-burning hot.
It’s easy to see how one might imagine Jaguar would pitch its i-Pace advantages over Tesla in a bullet point format:
Lower starting price than Tesla Model S, X and Performance 3.
Full U.S. $7,500 Federal tax credit available after the end of 2018.
Heads-up display.
360 degree camera, especially useful for off-road and parking.
Effective high-speed Automatic Emergency Braking.
Shorter car than S and X means easier to park.
Roof grab handles make it easier to get in and out compared to Model S.
Activity band is a key when you surf, swim or equivalent.
Charge port near the front of the car.
Air suspension lifts the car up to 90mm from its lowest setting, great for off road.
50cm wading depth means not only off-road, but no flood damage in nice areas.
Proper blind spot warning indicators by the A-pillars.
Four-zone air conditioning.
Available with upscale textile (vegan) interior.
Android Auto, Apple CarPlay and Amazon Alexa integration.
Off-road speed/slip control similar to Land Rover / Range Rover.
Won’t overheat on the racetrack when driven at extreme speeds requiring power.
Five years and 60,000 miles worth of maintenance included.
Of course, it’s not like Tesla doesn’t lack any advantage against Jaguar. It’s clear that Tesla currently has the better charging network. The flip side of this current fact, however, is that this advantage is in the process of being significantly neutralized. Networks in Europe as well as the U.S. (Electrify America) are deploying billions of dollars into new chargers, and Tesla’s current Supercharger advantage won’t be all that much of an issue 18 months from now: here.
Who is the typical U.S. customer for the Jaguar i-Pace?
In order to understand the product and its prospects for success, you should have an idea about its customer. I will describe two typical customers for the Jaguar i-Pace.
First, the Silicon Valley executive. This person might live in Atherton or Woodside. The office may be on Sand Hill Road or somewhere in the valley. Basically, the commute is between five and 25 miles each way. This person charges only at work, because it’s tax free, and why not? Annual income is around $1 million and net worth $15 million. This guy would never dream of driving more than 80 miles in a day, because that’s what airplanes are for. Rather, the purchase motivation is to buy the newest and most fashionable new EV in the market. The previous car was a Tesla, but it was a pain to own because it was in the shop all the time, and all of your friends already have one, so it’s nothing special anymore.
Second, the Beverly Hills housewife. This person drives 10 miles per day, mostly to Rodeo Drive and The Ivy on Robertson for a two-hour lunch. Charging takes place at home. The purchase motivation is the same as the Silicon Valley person above: It’s a fashion statement to own the hottest new EV on the market. Also, a car that can handle 20 inches worth of a flash flood without getting damaged. And as with the Silicon Valley executive, the previous car was a Tesla, where the door handles sometimes worked, when the car wasn’t actually in the shop.
The lingering question about the Jaguar i-Pace
I didn’t hear a single meaningful negative comment from any of the highly qualified automotive journalists who drove the Jaguar i-Pace yet, other than the network taking another year or two to build out. Rather, there was nervous “Tesla bankruptcy” laughter coming out the mouths of some. Basically, if a customer gets to experience the Jaguar i-Pace, why on Earth would they want a Tesla? That was the sentiment.
Based on that, Jaguar alone looks to take a chunk out of Tesla’s sales, starting in the coming months.
But wait. How many i-Pace units will Jaguar actually manufacture?
Well, therein resides the rub. Jaguar is not saying how many units it intends to manufacture, for any time period. It is keeping this card close to its vest - at least for now.
We can back into some near-term constraints for Jaguar’s i-Pace sales. Magna (NYSE: MGA ), which makes the car for Jaguar, has a 200,000 a year unit cap on its near-term production in Graz, Austria. Mercedes sold 22,000 G-Wagens last year, and it made 50,000 BMW 5-series there. That leaves us with 128,000 per year for Jaguar.
However, Jaguar splits its Graz allocation between the i-Pace and the E-Pace. It is not saying how it intends this split to evolve. Is it 50/50? Is it something radically different? As a baseline scenario, I would not assume that it would be more than 50%, so 64,000 per year, for the i-Pace. Of course, it could quite possibly be a lot less.
Then again, these production numbers - whatever they are now in the summer of 2018 - will evolve. Governments around the world are in the mood to force the market to consume more electric cars, so as a result, automakers are responding. Production numbers for EVs are going up, not down. Whatever number Jaguar had in mind as little as a year ago, it’s likely larger now, and could be larger yet soon enough. 20,000 a year could have gone to 40,000 now, on their way to 60,000. Who knows? The numbers will speak for themselves over the coming months and years.
Market share vs. market growth In this context, where the EV market is growing rapidly, Tesla could of course be at least a partial beneficiary despite massive market share losses for the Model S and X in the months to come. One single car - this Jaguar - that enters the market with demand a lot higher than supply may not sink Tesla’s ship with its own numbers alone.
However, the impact here is likely to be more psychological. Now that Jaguar has delivered a car that is - by the accounts of most journalists whose jobs it is to evaluate cars against each other - a superior electric car compared to Tesla, what about the other automakers?
Jaguar i-Pace is the first premium automaker to hit the market in a battle against Tesla. But it is not the last. Next up is Audi, and Mercedes will follow closer to the middle of 2019. And then we have Volvo around that time too, as well as Buick.
Perhaps not all of those cars from Audi, Mercedes, Volvo and Buick will be quite as good as the Jaguar. Or maybe they will. Perhaps even better! The point is, the competitive landscape is now starting to tighten around Tesla. It’s like watching a pack of hyenas attack a wildebeest, in 2019-2020.
Of course, we knew about all of these cars from Mercedes, Audi, Jaguar et al, already in 2014-2016, but the market has been too lazy to consider them. If there was ever proof that the market is not so much a discounting mechanism, but rather one focused on the most extreme short-term thinking, this may be the best example yet. It’s almost like a debt crisis: First, it’s ignored forever, and then it hits like a Titanic iceberg almost overnight.
For many of those who got drive the Jaguar i-Pace thus far, it feels like this was just such an iceberg. The crown of “best premium EV in the market” has just been passed from Tesla to Jaguar.
One final observation: We have been hearing from Tesla fans for over half a decade that “but did you drive it yet?” There was definitely a lot of truth to that. But now the tables have turned. Will Tesla fans dismiss the Jaguar i-Pace before they have driven it yet?
That would be as unwise now, as it was unwise then.
Disclosure: I am/we are short TSLA.
